preferences.reason: C's empty state explains the app and streak honestly, its week chart marks Sunday as in progress, and its book detail shows all four sessions.
B puts Start Session for Middlemarch right under the goal and lists every book with Log; A buries the action mid-screen and cramps the other books.
C's book detail shows the full session history and its chart flags today in progress; B loses sessions and its tab bar crowds the home indicator.
B's serif-set highlight quotation, warm paper ground and dog-ear motif give a reading voice; C is tidy but closer to a stock iOS template.
B pairs serif titles and reading text with the UI sans and carries a product motif; A is all generic sans with plain cover placeholders.
C's serif book titles, hatched in-progress bar and one-line app explanation on the empty state beat A's plainer type and thinner empty copy.
C keeps every target at 44 pt and its tab bar clear of the home indicator; B's small Log capsules and low tab bar miss both.
C marks Sunday in progress with a pattern, lists all three books with their last session, and its empty state explains the app; A compresses two books.
A's floating tab bar sits above the home indicator and its Today targets are full size; B has sub-44 Log buttons and a tab bar in the bottom inset.

briefs.notes: Judge notes (labels as judged, mapping above). J1: None of the three puts the recent highlight on Today's first screen. C's only contrast failure is 5.5 px cover placeholder text, which isn't primary text. All three follow the floating-tab-bar and glass-button pattern; I separated them mostly on task content and on how honest each state is. | J2: All three follow Liquid Glass placement: floating tab bar with separate search, glass back and more buttons, large titles. Differences are mostly identity and type setting. Only B puts the long quotation on a first screen and sets it as reading text. | J3: All three use iOS 26 patterns: large title, inset floating tab bar with separate Search, round glass nav buttons. None uses Material patterns or a bezel. The only measured contrast failure is C's decorative cover microtext. Differences on platform come down to targets, bottom-inset placement and how in-progress and below-goal status are encoded.

briefs.notes: Judge notes (labels as judged, mapping above). J1: All three restructure well around check-in (waiting room first, alerts on top of the detail panel), so they are close. B wins on the status system and the double booking. A is the cleanest but the least explicit. C has the strongest check-in action but minor clipping, and some legacy functions have no visible home. | J2: All three restructure the screen the same basic way: a waiting-room list, the clinician grid, then an alerts-first detail panel. Differences are in finish. C appears to use a hyperlegible face with slashed zeros, a good fit for reading MRNs and times, but the time labels wrap and long blocks show truncated footers. B has the most finished component vocabulary, though some cells cut off reasons with an ellipsis. A is clean but more generic. | J3: All three redesigns have clean fact sheets (0 AA failures, 0 small targets). The differences are in how status and type are encoded and in how legible the grid text is. C's time column wraps '8:00 AM' onto two lines. In all arms, secondary text in the grid runs close to 11px.
